steps.label: Do Now: Using a Model (1 of 2)
steps.content:
Do Now: Using a Model (1 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does a model need a rule as well as the start amount?Show the answer

The start is only where it begins. The rule says how it changes each week.

From 3.1: models and their parts.

Savings model
Rule: each week, add 15.
Start: 40 in the account.
Total: 3 marks

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: using a model

steps.text: This is a different model with the same three questions. Do the same steps with yours.
steps.visual:
Coin jar model
Rule: each week, add 8.
Start: 30 in the jar.

steps.text: Predict after 5 weeks. Begin with the start: 30.
steps.visual:
Start: 30
Rule: each week, add 8.
So far: 30

steps.text: The rule adds 8 once for every week. 5 weeks of 8 is 40.
steps.visual:
Start: 30
Rule: each week, add 8.
5 x 8 = 40

steps.text: Which part is "each week, add 8"? Ask: is it given at the start, does it say how to work something out, or is it worked out at the end?
It says how to work the answer out, so it is the rule. Ask the same three things about your part.
Someone types the start as 3, not 30. The model only knows what it is given, so it uses 3: 3 + 40 = 43.

steps.label: Do Now: What a Model Leaves Out (2 of 2)
steps.content:
Do Now: What a Model Leaves Out (2 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does a queue get longer when more cars arrive than go?Show the answer

Each minute, the cars that arrive are added and the cars that go are taken away. More in than out means it grows.

From 3.1: running a model, and what it leaves out.

Traffic light model
2 cars wait at the start.
6 cars arrive each minute.
The green light lets 4 go each minute.
Total: 2 marks

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: the traffic model

steps.text: This is a different traffic model, with two questions like yours. Use these steps on yours.
steps.visual:
Traffic light model
0 cars wait at the start.
7 cars arrive each minute.
The green light lets 3 go each minute.

steps.text: Each minute, add the cars that arrive: 7.
steps.visual:
Traffic light model
0 cars wait at the start.
7 cars arrive each minute.
The green light lets 3 go each minute.
+7 each minute

steps.text: Each minute, take away the cars that go: 3. So each minute the queue grows by 7 - 3 = 4.
steps.visual:
Traffic light model
0 cars wait at the start.
7 cars arrive each minute.
The green light lets 3 go each minute.
7 - 3 = 4 more each minute

steps.text: Start at the cars waiting at the start, then add 4 for every minute. After 4 minutes: 0 + 4 x 4 = 16.
steps.visual:
Traffic light model
0 cars wait at the start.
7 cars arrive each minute.
The green light lets 3 go each minute.
0 + 4 x 4 = 16 cars

steps.text: The model leaves out the drivers' names. Look at what the model works with: cars arriving and cars going.
steps.visual:
Traffic light model
0 cars wait at the start.
7 cars arrive each minute.
The green light lets 3 go each minute.

steps.text: Names are never added or taken away, so they cannot change the number waiting. The prediction stays at 16. Now ask this about your question.

steps.label: 3.2: Data Requirements for Models
steps.content:
Data Models and Collection

3.2: Data Requirements for Models

Year 8

  • Today: find the data a model needs.
  • The big question: why do different apps need different data?
Think → Pair → ShareA sat nav and a weather app run on the same phone. Why might they need different data?Show the answer

They do different jobs. Today we find out how the job decides the data.

steps.label: What Data Does a Model Need?
steps.content:
What Data Does a Model Need?

Think → Pair → SharePredict: which numbers must someone count before this model can run? Why?Show the worked answer

The cars waiting at 8 am, the cars that arrive each minute, the cars that go each minute, and the number of minutes.

Why? The rule uses each one. Without one of them, the rule cannot be worked out.

The data requirements of a model are the data it needs to work.

Traffic light model
It predicts the cars waiting at the end.
Rule: each minute, cars waiting = cars waiting + cars that arrive - cars that go.
  • Read the rule. Find each thing it uses.
  • Each one is data the model needs.
  • Data the rule never uses is not needed, like the colour of each car.

steps.label: Your Turn: Needed or Not?
steps.content:
Your Turn: Needed or Not?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy read the rule before you look at the options?Show the answer

The rule says exactly what the model works with. An option can sound sensible and still not be in the rule.

items.prompt: Rabbit model. Rule: each year, the rabbits double. Which data does it need?
options: The rabbits on the island now
The number of foxes on the island
items.explain: The rule only doubles the rabbits. It never uses foxes, size or weight, so the model does not need them.

items.prompt: Trip model. Rule: cost = price of the coach + price of one ticket x students going. Which data is NOT needed?
options: How far away the trip is
items.explain: The rule never uses the distance. The price of the coach is already in the rule.

steps.label: Compare: This Year's Data, Last Year's Data
steps.content:
Compare: This Year's Data, Last Year's Data

Think → Pair → ShareBoth use the same rule. Predict each cost. Why does only one match the real cost?Show the worked answer

A: 3000 + 150 x 40 = 9000. B: 3000 + 100 x 40 = 7000.

Why? Tickets cost 150 this year. B uses last year's price, so the rule gets the wrong number.

School trip model. Rule: cost = price of the coach + price of one ticket x number of students going.

Model A

Price of the coach3000
Price of one ticket this year150
Number of students going40
Cost?

Model B

Price of the coach3000
Price of one ticket last year100
Number of students going40
Cost?
  • The data must be about this system, now.
  • Old data, or data about something else, gives a wrong prediction.

steps.label: Activity 1: Choose the Data
steps.content:
Activity 1: Choose the Data

Think → Pair → ShareWhy run the model after you choose the data?Show the answer

The run shows what the rule really used. A blank or a wrong number shows up as a wrong prediction.

steps.label: Compare: All the Data, One Item Missing
steps.content:
Compare: All the Data, One Item Missing

Think → Pair → ShareBoth use the same rule. Predict each output. Why is B so far out when its rule is right?Show the worked answer

A: 2 + (7 - 4) x 5 = 17 cars. B: 2 + (7 - 0) x 5 = 37 cars.

Why? B has no number for the cars that go. The rule takes away 0 each minute, so no car ever leaves.

Traffic light model. Rule: each minute, cars waiting = cars waiting + cars that arrive - cars that go.

Model A: all the data

Cars waiting at 8 am2
Cars that arrive each minute7
Cars that go each minute4
Number of minutes5
Cars waiting at the end?

Model B: one item missing

Cars waiting at 8 am2
Cars that arrive each minute7
Cars that go each minuteblank
Number of minutes5
Cars waiting at the end?
  • A blank counts as 0, so the rule works out the wrong answer.
  • Data the rule never uses changes nothing, and takes time to collect.

steps.label: What If? Predict, Then Run It
steps.content:
What If? Predict, Then Run It

Think → Pair → ShareWhy predict before you run it?Show the answer

A prediction shows what you think the rule does. If the run is different, you find out which idea to fix.

steps.label: Explain: Why Missing Data Matters
steps.content:
Explain: Why Missing Data Matters

Think → Pair → ShareWhat makes an explanation worth 2 marks?Show the answer

Two points, where the second one follows from the first. Join them with so.

items.prompt: A traffic light model has this rule: each minute, cars waiting = cars waiting + cars that arrive - cars that go. It is not given the number of cars the green light lets go each minute. Explain why its prediction will be wrong.
items.modelAnswer: The rule takes away the cars that go, so it needs that number (1). With it blank, no cars go, so it predicts a queue that is too long (1).
scheme: The rule uses / needs the cars that go (it takes them away each minute)
With it missing (blank / 0) no cars leave, so the predicted queue is too long / too big / more than the real queue

steps.label: Different Applications, Different Data
steps.content:
Different Applications, Different Data

Think → Pair → SharePredict: does a sat nav need the air pressure? Why or why not?Show the worked answer

No.

Why? Air pressure does not change the journey time, so the sat nav never uses it.

An application (app) is a program that does a job for its users.

Weather app
It works out: the chance of rain tomorrow.
It needs: air pressure, how wet the air is, wind, where you are.
Sat nav
It works out: the fastest way and the journey time.
It needs: where you are, where you want to go, the roads, how fast the traffic is moving.
  • A different job means a different output.
  • A different output needs a different rule, so it needs different data.

steps.label: Compare: Same Data, Two Applications
steps.content:
Compare: Same Data, Two Applications

Think → Pair → ShareWhy would a fitness app need your heart rate, but a savings app would not?Show the answer

Heart rate changes the energy you used. It never changes the money you will have.

Weather appworks out the chance of rainneeds air pressure, how wet the air is, wind
Flight simulatorworks out how the plane movesneeds the control stick, engine power, wind

items.prompt: Why do both need the wind speed and direction?
options: Wind changes the rain and the plane's path
Wind is easy to measure, so both collect it
The simulator copies the weather app's data
Every application needs the same data
items.explain: Wind changes where the rain goes, and it pushes the plane.

items.prompt: Why does only the simulator need the control stick?
options: The weather app cannot measure the stick
Only the plane's path depends on the stick
The stick is part of every computer
The weather app is older than the simulator
items.explain: The stick moves the plane. It never changes the rain.

steps.label: Activity 2: Two Applications, Different Data
steps.content:
Activity 2: Two Applications, Different Data

Think → Pair → ShareWhy check each item against each application, one at a time?Show the answer

An item can matter to one application, to both, or to neither. Checking each one stops you guessing.

steps.label: Explain: Why Applications Need Different Data
steps.content:
Explain: Why Applications Need Different Data

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is "they need different data" not enough for 2 marks?Show the answer

It only repeats the question. A mark needs a reason, and the second mark needs a link to it.

items.prompt: A weather app and a sat nav run on the same phone. Explain why the two applications need different data.
items.modelAnswer: They work out different things: the chance of rain and the journey time (1). So their rules use different data, like air pressure and traffic speed (1).
scheme: They do different jobs / work out different outputs (the chance of rain; the journey time or the way)
So their rules use different data, with an example only one of them needs (air pressure / how wet the air is; where you want to go / traffic speed / the roads)

steps.label: Practice: Design the Data
steps.content:
Practice: Design the Data

Think → Pair → ShareWhy read the whole brief before you choose any data?Show the answer

Each part of the brief says something that changes the answer. Miss one part and the model misses data it needs.
